title: Design Patterns with Python Examples
description: Complete reference to all 23 Gang of Four design patterns using typed, Pythonic examples, selection guidance, trade-offs, implementation hints, and modern language alternatives.

sections.title: Pattern Foundations & Selection
sections.description: Patterns name recurring design forces; they are decision vocabulary, not mandatory class templates.

subtopics.title: Intent, Context, Forces & Consequences
subtopics.description: Apply a pattern only after identifying the varying responsibility, collaborators, constraints, and accepted costs.

codeBlocks.code:
1. Problem: what behavior or structure keeps changing?
2. Context: where does the problem occur and who owns it?
3. Forces: extensibility, consistency, latency, memory, testability
4. Candidate: which pattern resolves those forces?
5. Consequences: indirection, object count, lifecycle, debugging cost
6. Exit test: would a function, dict, closure, dataclass, or Protocol be simpler?

callouts.title: Patterns Are Not Goals
callouts.text: Introducing a pattern without present variation usually creates speculative abstractions. Start simple, observe pressure, then refactor toward a named pattern.

subtopics.title: Pythonic Pattern Toolkit
subtopics.description: Functions are objects, modules are singletons, protocols support structural typing, iterators are built in, decorators are syntax, and context managers encode setup/cleanup.

codeBlocks.code:
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterator
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
from functools import singledispatch, wraps
from typing import Protocol, Self

class Sender(Protocol):
    def send(self, message: str) -> None: ...

Transform = Callable[[str], str]

callouts.title: Prefer Structural Contracts
callouts.text: A typing.Protocol often expresses a role without forcing inheritance. Use ABCs when shared implementation, runtime registration, or enforced instantiation rules are genuinely required.

subtopics.description: Creational patterns vary construction, structural patterns vary composition, and behavioral patterns vary collaboration and algorithms.

sections.title: Creational Patterns (5)
sections.description: Separate clients from concrete construction decisions and object assembly rules.

subtopics.title: 1. Abstract Factory
subtopics.description: Create compatible families of related objects without exposing their concrete classes. Use when switching one product family must switch every related product consistently.

callouts.title: Family Consistency Is the Point
callouts.text: If only one product type varies, a simple factory function is enough. Abstract Factory earns its cost when multiple products must remain compatible.

subtopics.title: 2. Builder
subtopics.description: Construct a complex object step by step, separating assembly from representation. Useful for validated configuration, staged protocols, or multiple representations.

callouts.title: Dataclass May Be Enough
callouts.text: Prefer a dataclass with defaults or a keyword-only constructor when construction is simple. Builder helps when assembly is staged, conditional, validated across fields, or reused by a director.

subtopics.title: 3. Factory Method
subtopics.description: Let a base workflow defer one creation step to subclasses or collaborators. The creator uses the product through a stable contract.

callouts.title: Function Factories Are Often Better
callouts.text: If no creator workflow needs overriding, use create_encoder(format) or a registry dict. Factory Method specifically links polymorphic creation to an extensible creator operation.

subtopics.title: 4. Prototype
subtopics.description: Create objects by copying a configured exemplar when construction is expensive or runtime configuration matters more than class selection.

codeBlocks.code:
from copy import deepcopy
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace

@dataclass
class Report:
    title: str
    sections: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

prototype = Report("Monthly", ["Summary", "Metrics"])
independent = deepcopy(prototype)
renamed = replace(prototype, title="Weekly")  # shallow field reuse

callouts.title: Choose Copy Semantics Explicitly
callouts.text: Shallow copies share nested mutable objects; deep copies can duplicate resources or preserve relationships incorrectly. Implement __copy__/__deepcopy__ or a domain clone method when semantics matter.

subtopics.title: 5. Singleton
subtopics.description: Guarantee one accessible instance for a process or scope. In Python, a module, dependency container, or cached factory is usually clearer than overriding __new__.

callouts.title: Global State in Disguise
callouts.text: Singletons hide dependencies, couple tests through shared state, and are only single per process/interpreter—not across workers or machines. Inject the instance and scope it deliberately.

sections.title: Structural Patterns (7)
sections.description: Compose objects and interfaces while keeping responsibilities independently changeable.

subtopics.title: 6. Adapter
subtopics.description: Translate an existing incompatible interface into the contract a client expects. The adapter changes shape, names, units, or data representation.

callouts.title: Keep Translation at the Boundary
callouts.text: Convert vendor exceptions, units, and response models inside the adapter so vendor concepts do not leak into the domain.

subtopics.title: 7. Bridge
subtopics.description: Separate two independently varying dimensions—an abstraction and its implementation—so combinations grow additively rather than through a subclass explosion.

callouts.title: Bridge vs Adapter
callouts.text: Bridge is designed up front to vary two dimensions; Adapter repairs an interface mismatch, often around legacy or third-party code.

subtopics.title: 8. Composite
subtopics.description: Represent part-whole trees so clients treat leaves and containers through one interface. Useful for files, UI trees, rules, and organization structures.

callouts.title: Protect Tree Invariants
callouts.text: If cycles are invalid, prevent or detect them. Decide who owns parent links, mutation, traversal order, and error handling; a uniform interface can hide important leaf/container differences.

subtopics.title: 9. Decorator
subtopics.description: Wrap an object with the same contract to add behavior dynamically and compositionally. Python function decorators are a closely related language feature.

tabs.label: Object Decorator
Function Decorator

callouts.title: Preserve the Contract
callouts.text: A decorator must honor return values, exceptions, metadata, async behavior, and side-effect semantics. Wrapper order is observable and should be tested.

subtopics.title: 10. Facade
subtopics.description: Provide a cohesive high-level API over a complex subsystem. A facade coordinates collaborators but should not become a universal god object.

callouts.title: Facade vs Mediator
callouts.text: Facade gives clients a simpler one-way entry to a subsystem. Mediator coordinates peer components that otherwise communicate in a many-to-many network.

subtopics.title: 11. Flyweight
subtopics.description: Share immutable intrinsic state among many logical objects while callers supply extrinsic state. Useful only when measured object duplication is significant.

callouts.title: Bound the Cache
callouts.text: Interning unbounded user-controlled keys trades object duplication for a memory leak. Use bounded LRU/weak references or explicit lifecycle where the key space is not finite.

subtopics.title: 12. Proxy
subtopics.description: Stand in for another object to control access, lazily initialize, cross a remote boundary, cache, authorize, or instrument calls while preserving its interface.

callouts.title: Remote Proxies Are Not Local Objects
callouts.text: Network calls add latency, partial failure, retries, serialization, and idempotency. A transparent-looking proxy must not hide these semantics from API design.

sections.title: Behavioral Patterns (11)
sections.description: Assign algorithms, requests, state transitions, traversal, and collaboration to explicit roles.

subtopics.title: 13. Chain of Responsibility
subtopics.description: Pass a request through ordered handlers until one handles it or all contribute. Useful for validation, middleware, authorization, and event pipelines.

codeBlocks.code:
Handler = Callable[[Request, Callable[[Request], Response]], Response]

def compose(handlers: list[Handler], endpoint: Callable[[Request], Response]):
    next_handler = endpoint
    for handler in reversed(handlers):
        downstream = next_handler
        next_handler = lambda req, h=handler, n=downstream: h(req, n)
    return next_handler

app = compose([authenticate, rate_limit, log_request], endpoint)

callouts.title: Order and Termination Are Contracts
callouts.text: Document whether handlers may stop, transform, retry, or invoke downstream multiple times. Incorrect order can bypass authorization or duplicate side effects.

subtopics.title: 14. Command
subtopics.description: Encapsulate a request as an object so it can be queued, logged, retried, authorized, composed, or undone independently of the invoker.

callouts.title: Undo Needs Captured Reality
callouts.text: An inverse operation is not always true undo. Capture prior state, handle external changes, and define transaction boundaries; remote side effects may require compensation rather than reversal.

subtopics.title: 15. Interpreter
subtopics.description: Represent a small language grammar as expressions that evaluate against a context. Suitable for limited, stable DSLs—not general-purpose parsing.

callouts.title: Use Parser Tools as Grammar Grows
callouts.text: Precedence, diagnostics, ambiguity, optimization, and untrusted input rapidly outgrow a class-per-rule design. Use a proper parser/AST and sandbox evaluation; never eval untrusted text.

subtopics.title: 16. Iterator
subtopics.description: Traverse a collection without exposing representation. Python's iterator protocol and generators are the idiomatic implementation.

callouts.title: Iterators Are Stateful and One-Pass
callouts.text: iter(generator) returns the same exhausted object. Return a fresh generator from __iter__, document mutation during traversal, and close resource-backed generators deterministically.

subtopics.title: 17. Mediator
subtopics.description: Centralize collaboration among peer objects so they do not reference and coordinate each other directly. Useful for dialogs, workflows, and bounded event coordination.

callouts.title: Avoid a God Mediator
callouts.text: Split mediators by cohesive workflow. If every component event and business rule accumulates in one coordinator, coupling has moved rather than decreased.

subtopics.title: 18. Memento
subtopics.description: Capture and restore an object's state without exposing its internal representation. Useful for undo, checkpoints, editors, and simulations.

callouts.title: Snapshots Need Limits and Versions
callouts.text: Large snapshots consume memory and serialized snapshots couple to schema. Consider deltas, bounded history, compression, versioning, and explicit handling of external resources.

subtopics.title: 19. Observer
subtopics.description: Notify subscribers when a subject changes without hard-coding consumers. Useful for in-process domain notifications and UI bindings.

callouts.title: Define Delivery Semantics
callouts.text: Specify sync/async delivery, ordering, error isolation, reentrancy, unsubscribe lifetime, and backpressure. Strong subscriber references can leak owners; distributed events require a durable broker, not this pattern alone.

subtopics.title: 20. State
subtopics.description: Delegate behavior to an object representing the current state so transitions replace large conditional branches and invalid operations become explicit.

callouts.title: State vs Strategy
callouts.text: State usually changes internally as the object's lifecycle progresses and each state controls valid transitions. Strategy is normally selected externally to vary an algorithm.

subtopics.title: 21. Strategy
subtopics.description: Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms behind one contract so the client can select or inject policy independently of the workflow.

tabs.label: Callable Strategy
Protocol Strategy

callouts.title: Use a Function for Stateless Policy
callouts.text: A callable is the simplest Python strategy. Use a class when the algorithm needs configuration, dependencies, state, several related methods, or a richer contract.

subtopics.title: 22. Template Method
subtopics.description: Define an algorithm skeleton in a base class while subclasses override selected steps and hooks without changing the workflow order.

callouts.title: Inheritance Couples the Workflow
callouts.text: Document required super calls, hook order, and invariants. Prefer composition/Strategy when steps must vary at runtime or subclasses would override many interdependent hooks.

subtopics.title: 23. Visitor
subtopics.description: Add operations across a stable object structure without modifying every element class for each operation. Classic double dispatch trades easy operations for harder new element types.

tabs.label: Classic Visitor
Python singledispatch

callouts.title: Choose the Stable Axis
callouts.text: Visitor fits when element types are stable and new operations are frequent. If new element variants are frequent, methods/pattern matching or a different data representation may be easier.

sections.title: Comparisons, Combinations & Production Review
sections.description: Distinguish similar patterns, combine only compatible responsibilities, and test the added indirection.

subtopics.title: Commonly Confused Patterns
subtopics.description: Compare intent before comparing class diagrams.

codeBlocks.code:
Adapter changes an interface; Decorator adds behavior; Proxy controls access
Bridge separates planned dimensions; Adapter integrates an existing mismatch
Strategy swaps an algorithm; State changes behavior with lifecycle state
Facade simplifies a subsystem; Mediator coordinates peer collaboration
Factory Method varies one creation hook; Abstract Factory creates product families
Builder assembles stepwise; Prototype copies configured exemplars
Command represents a request; Memento represents captured state
Composite models a tree; Chain models ordered request handling

callouts.title: Intent Beats Shape
callouts.text: Several patterns wrap an object or use composition. Name the pattern from the force it resolves, not from superficial code structure.

subtopics.title: Useful Pattern Combinations
subtopics.description: Real designs often combine patterns, but each should retain one clear reason to exist.

codeBlocks.code:
Abstract Factory + Bridge → compatible implementations across dimensions
Composite + Iterator + Visitor → tree storage, traversal, and operations
Command + Memento → undoable actions with prior-state snapshots
State + Strategy → lifecycle state selects configurable algorithms
Facade + Adapter → stable subsystem API over vendor integrations
Proxy + Decorator → access control plus orthogonal instrumentation
Observer + Mediator → notifications feed a bounded workflow coordinator

callouts.title: Avoid Pattern Stacks by Default
callouts.text: Every layer adds naming, navigation, testing, and failure semantics. Add combinations incrementally in response to distinct forces, not to reproduce a catalog architecture.

subtopics.title: Testing Pattern-Based Designs
subtopics.description: Test contracts, substitutions, ordering, transitions, cleanup, and failure policy introduced by indirection.

codeBlocks.code:
Factories/builders: every variant, invariant, invalid configuration
Adapters/proxies/decorators: contract parity and exception translation
Composite/iterator/visitor: empty/deep trees, traversal order, cycles
Chain/middleware: order, short-circuit, downstream call count
Command/memento: execute/undo, compensation, bounded history
Observer/mediator: unsubscribe, reentrancy, subscriber failure
State: transition table and invalid transitions
Strategy/template: shared contract suite for every implementation

callouts.title: Contract Test Suites
callouts.text: Run the same behavioral tests against every implementation of a Protocol—real, adapter, proxy, decorator, and fake—to detect semantic drift.

subtopics.title: Pattern Selection Checklist
subtopics.description: Confirm current pressure, clearer ownership, preserved semantics, and an exit path before accepting abstraction cost.

codeBlocks.code:
□ The recurring problem and varying axis are concrete
□ A function/dict/dataclass/closure/Protocol is insufficient
□ Pattern intent is documented in domain language
□ Object lifetime and ownership are explicit
□ Error, cancellation, ordering, and concurrency semantics are defined
□ Contracts are smaller than their implementations
□ Extension does not require editing a central conditional everywhere
□ New indirection improves testing or substitution
□ Performance/memory costs are measured where relevant
□ The pattern does not hide network or transaction boundaries
□ A simpler refactor path remains possible
□ Team members can explain why this pattern fits

callouts.title: Delete Patterns That Lost Their Force
callouts.text: Requirements change. If only one implementation remains and variation is unlikely, collapsing an abstraction can improve the design.
